https://www.politico.eu/article/mykhailo.text: KYIV — Ukraine’s popular former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has emerged as a new rival to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — but his call for an election is facing immediate blowback. In a video address on Tuesday night, he zeroed in on topics he knew would strike a public chord in one of the most direct internal challenges to Zelenskyy since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He complained that corruption was undermining the war effort and protested about centralized and opaque decision-making in the Zelenskyy administration — for which he worked until only last month. However, Fedorov’s unexpected appeal for the nation to go to the ballot box sparked immediate retorts across the political spectrum. Critics insisted such an election would be banned by Ukraine’s martial law, would be impossible to organize in wartime, would play into Russia’s hands and would sow division when national unity remains vital. Advertisement Advertisement Zelenskyy still commands broad support as a war leader, and his allies pointed out that, regardless of public frustration, there are limits to how much he can reveal about the inner workings of the state when national survival is at stake. Fedorov’s emergence as a rival to Zelenskyy was accelerated by his shock dismissal as defense minister last month. The 35-year-old built up a strong following for spearheading Ukraine’s success in using new technologies — from cyberattacks to drones — to damage Russia. His ejection from office sparked immediate protests , with thousands of people taking to the streets, calling for his reinstatement or for Zelenskyy to properly explain the decision to fire him. In his address on Tuesday night, Fedorov delivered a thinly veiled criticism of Zelenskyy’s management style, referring to his peremptory approach to hiring and firing. “People cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made. Why some reforms move forward while others are blocked. Why decisions needed on the frontlines today spend months circulating through government offices,” Fedorov said. “It is dangerous when society develops the feeling that the main criterion for an appointment is not professionalism, results, or the ability to transform the country, but personal loyalty to the system,” added the former minister, who had himself been viewed as a Zelenskyy loyalist for seven years. Advertisement Advertisement Election backlash A top official in Zelenskyy’s office, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about Fedorov’s move, had little time for the criticism that the president should explain his actions publicly. “The president cannot just explain his hiring choices to the public during war, as those are matters of national security. And it’s his right to decide whom to appoint as his defense minister and whom to fire,” they said. The official was also scathing about the possibility of holding an election in the face of devastating Russian attacks: “Let’s wait out another massive Russian ballistic attack and then go vote,” the person added, sarcastically. Olga Aivazovska, head of Ukraine’s election watchdog OPORA, also stressed the practical obstacles to an election, insisting that there were “hundreds of scenarios and actions” that the Russians could use to undermine the electoral process. Roman Lozynskyi, a parliamentarian from the opposition liberal Holos party and deputy head of the state management committee, feared the call for elections could prove disastrously divisive. “There is zero positive for the country. Don’t be happy that you will have candidates in the post-war elections. You still have to live to see them,” he said. “People understand that elections during the war are in the enemy’s hands. That it will be a war of all against all.” Advertisement Advertisement Even one of the leaders of the protest movement, war veteran Dmytro Koziatysnkyi, said he didn’t want to see elections during wartime. “I am also very afraid of the disunity of society during the electoral process and how this may affect the course of the war,” he said. Far from bolstering Fedorov’s political future, the call for an election could even count against him. Economist Timothy Ash, who frequently writes on Ukraine, suggested the ex-minister had made “an extraordinary political error of judgement which some would likely use against him if he ever pitches in to run as president in the future.” Volodymyr Fesenko, a political analyst based in Kyiv, conceded Zelenskyy had become accustomed to “acting like in business,” defined by “single-man leadership” and “quick decisions,” but argued that the president was hardly acting out of step with any other major international leader. “When his critics say he should appoint professionals instead of loyalists, they sound right but naive at the same time. Even in the West, unless we are talking about coalition governments, such an approach does not work. Any serious politician … and especially in a country like ours, will appoint trusted loyalists,” Fesenko added. Fesenko also defended Zelenskyy’s record in appointing senior officials. He noted that Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, new commander-in-chief, Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi , as well as new Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara , all had positive reputations, even among Zelenskyy’s top critics in parliament. Advertisement Advertisement Indeed, Khmara was confirmed in his new role to succeed Fedorov by a parliamentary vote on Wednesday, by 312 lawmakers out of 392. ‘People want change’ Fedorov is certainly popular. A poll from the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology said earlier this month that 63 percent of people saw him as trustworthy — a score that put him second only to former military supremo Valeryi Zaluzhnyi, who is now ambassador to the U.K. But none of that put Zelenskyy, who scored a robust 56 percent, out of the picture. In line with Fedorov’s attack on a lack of transparency in the centralized state, another survey found dwindling sympathy for Zelenskyy using his powers to intervene over other state authorities. The poll found that 79 percent of people in 2022 — the year of Russia’s full-scale invasion — thought the president could override the constitution’s division of powers, but that had slipped to 52 percent in May 2026. “People are placing all responsibility for the course of the war on the president. Because of this, the president feels the need to make all these decisions independently, which is against Ukraine’s constitution and legislative procedures. As a result, one person, the president, has a huge number of completely different tasks, incentives, requirements,” said Yurii Hudymenko, head of the Public Anti-Corruption Council at Ukraine’s defense ministry. Corruption is also a hot topic, as Fedorov identified. Last year, Zelenskyy signed a law to strip Ukraine’s national anti-corruption watchdogs of their procedural independence, only to then backtrack on that decision when it faced criticism from the EU and protests at home. Advertisement Advertisement Later, his former business partner and allies were implicated in a $100 million corruption scheme in the state nuclear energy sector — a scandal that forced Zelenskyy to fire his faithful No. 2, Andriy Yermak. Yermak was charged with corruption and is standing trial. Several of Zelenskyy’s top allies are also under investigation for corruption, including former Ukrainian Ambassador to the U.S. Olga Stefanishyna , while watchdogs complain they still face tremendous pressure and surveillance when investigating top officials. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy fired Iryna Mudra as deputy head of his office, hours after anti-corruption watchdogs searched her workplace as part of a sweeping probe into an alleged criminal organization. Yaroslav Zheleznyak, MP from opposition party Holos, and a prominent Zelenskyy critic, said the cumulative weight of these problems would ultimately count against the president. He predicted Zelenskyy would suffer the fate of British wartime leader Winston Churchill and lose an election during the tail end of the war. “No matter the competitors, Zaluzhnyi, [Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo] Budanov, Fedorov or someone else, I think we will get the situation like in 2019, when anyone but the incumbent will win in the second round. In this case, this is very much a Churchill story, when a guy who won the war got voted out,” Zheleznyak said. Advertisement “People want change,” he added. Oleksandr Saienko, expert at the Center for Political and Legal Reforms, said it was possible to avert a political crisis even without elections, but that would mean shifting some decision-making back to parliament and other state authorities. “The subjectivity of the parliament must be restored both in terms of the legislative process and parliamentary control. The government must become the main center for the formation of state policy,” he said. “The pause on reform of the judicial system and law enforcement agencies, public administration, must be lifted and people should get a real sense of justice and protection.”

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Georgia Cook leaving the NSW supreme court after giving evidence at the double murder trial of former NSW police office Beau Lamarre-Condon. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP View image in fullscreen Georgia Cook leaving the NSW supreme court after giving evidence at the double murder trial of former NSW police office Beau Lamarre-Condon. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP Sydney Beau Lamarre-Condon told friend if he killed anyone he’d dump belongings in bin and take bodies to bushland, court hears Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024 – nine months after discussion with friend Georgia Cook Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.15 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Sydney police officer told a friend he would hide the bodies of anyone he killed in bushland and put their belongings in a dumpster, months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a court has been told. Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting the couple with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. At his double murder trial on Monday, Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court about a dinner in May 2023. Disguised as an UberEats rider, Beau Lamarre-Condon enters his ex’s home. Moments later, three gun shots ring out Read more The brief relationship between Baird and Lamarre-Condon had ended when the accused asked her what she would do if he told her he’d killed someone , Cook told the jury. He then asked what she would do if she killed someone and what she would do with their bodies, the court heard. Cook responded she had no idea. She said on Monday that Lamarre-Condon replied: “After I’d killed them I would take their stuff, I would put it in a dumpster, and I would take their bodies in bushland where nobody would ever find them.” Asked about her response, Cook said the situation in 2023 felt “very surreal”. “I didn’t know whether to believe anything I’d heard, or whether it was true,” she told the jury. “Hearing a person of power in the police force [say that] – it felt like I didn’t have anywhere to go and I was really scared by what I had heard.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon in the NSW supreme court. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP After Lamarre-Condon allegedly shot Baird and Davies in February 2024, he dumped Baird’s bloodied belongings and furniture into a skip bin in Cronulla, the prosecution said during its opening statement last week. The two bodies were found on the fence line of a Greek orthodox monastery in remote bushland in Bungonia – about 200km from Paddington. Cook on Friday told the court that Lamarre-Condon told her he had been watching Baird from outside his home. The crown alleged in its opening that the police officer began planning to murder Baird in early 2024. The defence team has claimed he was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an UberEats rider and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings. The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues. https://www.theyeshivaworld.com/news/gen.text: NATO ON EDGE: Poland Boosts Ukraine Border Security As Russian Strikes Move Closer September 14, 2026 5:30 pm No Comments Poland is strengthening security along its border with Ukraine following Russian drone strikes near Polish territory, including attacks within kilometers of the frontier, the Associated Press reports. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Moscow appears prepared to intensify operations close to Ukraine’s borders with European countries. Tusk said Poland cannot rule out the possibility that the escalation could eventually affect Polish territory. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also said the Polish military recovered what was believed to be a Russian military drone from the Baltic Sea. Polish officials said intelligence indicated that Russia could target border points and intensify sabotage operations inside European countries in an effort to weaken Western support for Ukraine. Tusk indicated that Warsaw would consult NATO allies about preparations for a possible joint response. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte responded by pledging increased support for Ukraine and stronger defenses along NATO’s eastern flank as concern grows over Russian military activity increasingly close to alliance territory. https://baltic-review.com/riga-precision.text: Share Tweet 0 Riga’s National Library is hosting the Precision Medicine Networking Forum on October 8–9, 2026. A meeting point for personalised healthcare Riga is hosting the fifth Precision Medicine Networking Forum on October 8–9, bringing researchers and healthcare professionals together at the Conference Centre of the National Library of Latvia. The event is listed by Research Latvia, the national science-communication platform, as a two-day forum aimed primarily at researchers. The meeting comes as precision medicine continues to connect several areas that have traditionally developed in parallel: laboratory science, clinical decision-making, health data, medical education and innovation. Rather than presenting a single technology as a solution, the Riga programme is structured around several research and application fields, allowing participants to compare methods and discuss how discoveries can move closer to patient care. Several research tracks under one roof According to the programme information published by the American Chamber of Commerce in Latvia, the 2026 forum includes three parallel tracks. They cover functional precision medicine, cancer genetics, CAR-T therapies, cardiogenetics, artificial intelligence, microbiome research, biobanking and large-scale health and omics data. These subjects represent different parts of the same wider question: how can information about an individual’s biology be used responsibly to support prevention, diagnosis or treatment? Genetic information may help doctors understand inherited risks. Molecular and microbiome research can add detail to the picture of a patient’s condition. Data systems and artificial intelligence may assist researchers in identifying patterns, while biobanks provide carefully collected material for future studies. The value of a forum such as this is not limited to headline discoveries. Precision medicine depends on less visible work as well: agreeing on standards, improving data quality, training specialists, protecting patient information and creating systems through which researchers and hospitals can cooperate. Those practical questions are especially important for smaller research ecosystems seeking to build international partnerships without losing the ability to develop their own expertise. Latvia’s research and innovation ecosystem in focus The Riga event also has a clear national dimension. The organisers say that the programme, developed together with the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia, will highlight funding opportunities and the development of a precision-medicine ecosystem. That puts scientific exchange alongside questions of research financing, commercialisation and cooperation between universities, medical institutions and companies. For Latvia, this kind of connection can help give visibility to local researchers while also making it easier for international specialists to identify potential partners. The event is being held in English, although individual sessions may take place in Latvian, according to the official Research Latvia listing. The format therefore serves both domestic participants and a wider professional audience. Rīga Stradiņš University’s events calendar places the forum within a particularly active week for medical education and research. The university is also listing Psychology Days from October 6 to 9 and a seminar on the difficulty of translating biomarker discoveries into patient care, held on October 7. Taken together, the schedule reflects a broader interest in linking scientific evidence with practical healthcare and professional training. From discussion to future cooperation The forum is not presented as a promise of immediate medical breakthroughs. Its more measurable contribution is the creation of a setting in which specialists can exchange findings, identify shared challenges and develop future cooperation. Participants may also receive continuing medical education credits, according to the event information published by the American Chamber of Commerce in Latvia. A related Virtual Reality and Healthcare Europe Symposium is taking place in Riga on October 8–9, with sessions at Turība University and the National Library. Its programme includes medical education, immersive technology, digital health and applied research, and its organisers say attendees have access to the precision-medicine forum on October 9. The parallel programme broadens the week’s focus from biological data to the tools used to train professionals and deliver care. For visitors, the National Library provides a visible civic setting for a conversation that is often associated with specialist laboratories. For Latvia’s research community, the gathering offers a chance to present local expertise, build networks and consider how emerging medical knowledge can be translated into better-informed practice. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Mayor Olivia Chow delivers a speech after being re-elected for a second term in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on 26 October 2026. Photograph: Mert Alper Dervis/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Mayor Olivia Chow delivers a speech after being re-elected for a second term in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on 26 October 2026. Photograph: Mert Alper Dervis/Anadolu/Getty Images Toronto Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives Tightly fought election saw record turnout as incumbent mayor ran against her rival Brad Bradford Leyland Cecco in Toronto Tue 27 Oct 2026 16.23 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 17.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The mayor of Toronto , Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressive councillors. The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13 percentage point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared to his 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city. Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. On Monday night, she thanked her supporters and Bradford. “I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.” Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023 . Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed. While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years. Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending. In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers other vulnerable institutions. In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.” Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost. Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in a fierce battle over the city’s bike lanes. Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan, a well-known advocate for unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on city council. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/pier.text: Aproximativ 490.000 de soldaţi ruşi au murit în aproape cinci ani de război în Ucraina, potrivit unor surse media independente din Rusia, care citează statistici scurse de hackeri din Belarus şi Ucraina, relatează EFE. Conform datelor portalurilor independente ruse Meduza şi Mediazona , alţi 230.000 de militari sunt daţi dispăruţi. Publicațiile fac calculul și ajung la 720.000 - cel mai probabil numărul morților. Pentru moment nu se cunoaşte oficial numărul celor mutilaţi în luptă, deşi unele surse media vorbesc despre zeci de mii de soldaţi. Deşi Rusia nu a anunţat cifre oficiale ale morţilor din septembrie 2022, instituţii media independente - precum Vajnîe Istorii - estimează că armata sa suferă pierderi de ordinul a 600 de oameni zilnic. La sfârşitul anului 2025, Meduza şi Mediazona estimau, în cadrul anchetei lor comune, că numărul pierderilor armatei ruse se ridică la 352.000 de morţi. BBC, la rândul său, a precizat în decembrie 2025 că, în acel an, în Ucraina ar fi murit peste 33.000 de militari ruşi, conform informaţiilor din surse deschise. Statul Major rus susţine că partea adversă pierde aproape 1.000 de oameni pe zi în luptele cu trupele ruse. SUA au trimis peste 1.000 de militari la granița cu Belarus. More on this topic Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the sticking points in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, impeachment proceedings against U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Israeli efforts to form a new government. Big Optimism, Little Progress Russia, Ukraine, and the United States kicked off trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday for the first time in roughly nine months. Day 1 of the two-day conference largely focused on security guarantees for Kyiv in what U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner characterized as an initial step toward building momentum for future dialogue. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the sticking points in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, impeachment proceedings against U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Israeli efforts to form a new government. Big Optimism, Little Progress Russia, Ukraine, and the United States kicked off trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday for the first time in roughly nine months. Day 1 of the two-day conference largely focused on security guarantees for Kyiv in what U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner characterized as an initial step toward building momentum for future dialogue. Tuesday’s conversations were “constructive and quite substantive,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who did not attend the talks, wrote on Telegram. Lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky similarly expressed hope that this week’s dialogue will “allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.” But while negotiators are projecting cautious optimism, neither side appears willing to make concessions, and significant breakthroughs remain out of reach. Two key sticking points continue to hamper the ongoing peace talks. Ukraine and its European allies insist on an immediate cease-fire before negotiating a wider settlement; Russia, however, rejects such a truce, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arguing that Brussels is just trying to “buy time” for Kyiv. Ukraine also opposes any demands for it to cede territory to Russia, whereas Moscow wants Kyiv to withdraw from the four Russian-occupied regions of the Donbas. “Nobody believes that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will stop if we leave the Donbas,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Tuesday. “He will pause. And then he will return in a year, two, or five years. And who will be to blame?” Battle lines have not changed substantially in recent months, and just hours before negotiations began in Abu Dhabi, Russia launched overnight attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, causing outages in six regions. Moscow has repeatedly targeted Kyiv’s power grid in an effort to freeze Ukraine into submission ahead of what is expected to be another cold winter. But outside pressures could force Moscow and Kyiv to ramp up peacemaking efforts. Prolonged fighting has strained Russia’s wartime economy, Ukraine’s weapons arsenal remains dangerously low on U.S.-made interceptors, and European nations appear increasingly focused on addressing Black Sea security concerns. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged $56 million to help Bulgaria and Romania launch a Black Sea maritime security hub in the face of deadly drone attacks on cargo ships. Despite these influences, the likelihood of an imminent peace deal appears to be slim. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday during the G-7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris. “It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.” Today’s Most Read The Experts Are Taking Their Revenge Again by David Milne Hegseth’s Leadership Has Damaged the Pentagon by Kori Schake Who Will Succeed Xi Jinping? by Deng Yuwen What We’re Following Hegseth fights back. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a defiant rebuttal on Tuesday of bipartisan efforts to impeach him for “high crimes and misdemeanors” related to his execution of the Iran war, deadly strikes on alleged drug boats, and capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said, referring to outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who has led the impeachment push against him on the grounds that Hegseth has abused his power and endangered members of the armed forces. The defense secretary went on to defend his policy decisions, champion military recruitment, and characterize the proceedings as a direct attack on the armed forces. “These resolutions are a farce,” Hegseth said. “They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders.” The comments, made during Hegseth’s first news conference at the Pentagon in six months, came just hours before the House of Representatives was scheduled to hold an initial procedural vote on the impeachment articles. Still, the Trump administration is not shying away from the fight. “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday. Deadlocked coalition talks. The Israeli Knesset swore in its new lawmakers on Tuesday, just days after President Isaac Herzog tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government. “You must do everything to avoid a repeat election,” Herzog told lawmakers during the swearing-in ceremony. But with coalition-building efforts still deadlocked, Israel’s incoming parliamentary term could be cut short if both Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fail to form a governing bloc. Eisenkot’s fragmented opposition has the backing of 67 members in the 120-seat Knesset, compared to Netanyahu’s 46 supporters. However, Eisenkot’s path to power remains uncertain, as many of his mainstream Jewish partners have balked at the idea of entering into a formal alliance with Arab-led parties. Without the latter group’s 19 seats, Eisenkot’s bloc lacks the 61-seat majority that it needs to solidly oppose Netanyahu. But with them, Eisenkot could be risking his long-term political future ; the only time that an Israeli governing coalition has included an Arab-led party, the alliance held together for just a little more than a year. In the meantime, Eisenkot has already vowed to replace the Knesset’s speaker, Amir Ohana. Ohana is a Netanyahu loyalist, so removing him would deal a significant blow to the right wing’s legislative agenda. The opposition hopes to replace him with Matan Kahana, a senior figure in Eisenkot’s party, but the date for such a vote has yet to be determined. Spotty record. The United Nations Human Rights Council (HRC) agreed on Tuesday to further delay a regular review of the United States’ human rights record after Washington was set to become the first U.N. member to fully reject it. The process will now reconvene in January. Every four to five years, the world’s top human rights body examines the records of all 193 U.N. member states to determine whether governments are adhering to international human rights standards. According to a new report by the office of the U.N. high commissioner for human rights, the United States appears to have violated several of these norms, from targeting civilian infrastructure in Iran to imposing sanctions on the International Criminal Court that “could undermine accountability for war crimes and crimes against humanity.” The White House pulled out of the council last year, alleging anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and it has repeatedly skipped its HRC review appointments. “[W]e give no credibility to the agency,” a State Department spokesperson told The Associated Press , calling the council an “irredeemable body” that “makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values.’” Odds and Ends The Booker Prize for fiction was awarded on Monday to The End of Everything , a dystopian satirical novel by British writer M. John Harrison that explores how difficult it is to understand a deteriorating world when you are right in the middle of it. This was the first time that the prestigious award went to a bona fide science fiction writer, though Harrison maintains that the recognition signals how the era of “genres as fences and boxes, pigeonholes, is over.” British fantasy and science fiction is having something of a moment in literary prizes, FP’s James Palmer told World Brief. Harrison’s disciple, China Miéville, recently won the prestigious Goldsmiths Prize for his more than 1,200-page paranormal Cold War epic The Rouse .
